A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FHBI method and VTAB-1K study. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification accuracy, calibration, runtime, particle-count, sharpness, and gradient-diversity experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds baseline comparisons, kernel analyses, and larger-model resource measurements.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains the same kernel-coupled perturbation and descent updates, posterior target, and SAM/SVGD special cases. Additional theory and alternative-kernel experiments do not change the proposed FHBI procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions use ImageNet-21K pretraining and the same 19 VTAB-1K datasets across Natural, Specialized, and Structured domains. New appendix experiments use subsets of these datasets; the larger backbone changes model configuration rather than dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: Tables 1 and 2 add SADA-JEM and SA-BNN to both accuracy and calibration comparisons, retaining all seven earlier baselines. These closely related sharpness-aware Bayesian methods substantially strengthen the comparison relevant to FHBI's distinctive contribution. SA-BNN's underlying work was cited in v1 but was not evaluated there.

E3.justification: New appendix protocols compare RBF with a degree-10 polynomial kernel, extend the sensitivity sweep to sigma values 0.1 and 2.5, and compare ViT-B/16 with ViT-L/16 resource usage on three retained datasets. These are additional configurations; the existing hyperparameter selections and augmentation procedures are retained.

E4.justification: Appendices B.2-B.4 add analyses of kernel-family dependence, larger-model memory and computational requirements, and RBF-lengthscale sensitivity. These substantially broaden the robustness and scalability questions examined. The original particle-count analysis moves to Appendix B.1, while the sharpness and gradient-diversity analysis remains.

E5.justification: Both versions report five FHBI runs with means and standard deviations, and Table 1 retains the same uncertainty values. This disclosure moves to Appendix C.1. No new seed-reporting practice, confidence intervals, or significance tests are introduced.

E6.justification: All existing rows in Tables 1-2 remain numerically unchanged, including FHBI's 73.7 average accuracy and 0.12 ECE. New SADA-JEM/SA-BNN rows report average accuracies of 72.1/68.1 and ECEs of 0.19/0.20. Tables 4-7 add kernel, resource, and sensitivity results, including RBF versus polynomial averages of 86.8 versus 86.5. Table 6's metric and units are ambiguous because its caption conflicts with the surrounding training-time description.

T1.justification: v2 adds Proposition 4.1 and its proof characterizing the population posterior through regularized expected loss. Theorems 4.2-4.3 and Appendix A substantially revise the bounds with explicit sample-size/confidence dependence, Hölder and kernel-boundedness assumptions, removal of approximation remainders, and a VC-based argument replacing v1's constant normalizer-gap bound. These are substantive mathematical changes. However, Appendix A.2's justification for removing the approximation remainder contradicts its displayed 1/M dependence.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list broaden the stated empirical superiority claim from seven to nine baselines; the conclusion updates its earlier count of six to nine. The central claims about functional sharpness, extending generalization analysis to RKHS, and the FHBI sampler remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds a regularized-risk interpretation of the population posterior and interprets the new baseline comparisons as distinguishing FHBI from simpler SAM-based combinations. It also interprets kernel experiments as evidence of robustness and attributes extreme-lengthscale degradation to overfitting or underfitting. The existing multiple-model memory limitation remains.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly identifies the Gaussian/RBF kernel and adds resource measurements, retaining hyperparameters and augmentation code in Appendix C. It removes FHBI's code/configuration/log link and reproducibility statement, plus the explicit 1,000-example and 80/20 split description. The four-particle disclosure now covers Bayesian methods rather than all methods except AdamW and full finetuning; this does not establish that SAM's actual setting changed.

R1.justification: v2 adds Pham et al. (2025), Yang et al. (2023), and Shalev-Shwartz and Ben-David (2014), and expands discussion of related sharpness-aware Bayesian approaches. Proposition 4.1 is explicitly positioned relative to Nguyen et al. (2023). Other reference changes largely update publication metadata or consolidate duplicate citations.

P1.justification: v2 edits wording, adopts population-posterior terminology, updates author and venue information, and adds acknowledgments and an impact statement. It reorganizes appendices into proofs, additional experiments, and experimental details, moving the particle-count study out of the main text. Most existing narrative and the main section sequence are retained.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from a predominantly single-column layout to a two-column conference format, with extensive resizing and relocation of displays. Tables 1-2 gain comparator rows, Table 3 is reformatted and moved, and Tables 4-7 are added. Existing schematics and plotted findings are retained, with the runtime figure moved to the appendix.

improvement.justification: The added SA-BNN/SADA-JEM comparisons and targeted kernel/scalability analyses improve scrutiny of FHBI's empirical advantage and practical limitations. This gain is tempered by removal of code/configuration/log access information, Table 6's ambiguous resource metric, and unresolved justification of the stronger theoretical bounds: Appendix A.2 removes an approximation remainder using a limit inconsistent with its 1/M dependence. The revision provides useful additional evidence without establishing a comprehensive improvement in rigor or reproducibility.
